claim: The hippocampus is linked with both sleep and memory.
source: The hippocampus is linked with both sleep and memory, but there is debate about whether a salient aspect of sleep – dreaming – requires its input.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the abstract without specific supporting data or citations in this sentence.

claim: There is debate about whether dreaming requires hippocampal input.
source: The hippocampus is linked with both sleep and memory, but there is debate about whether a salient aspect of sleep – dreaming – requires its input.
evidence: This acknowledges an ongoing scientific debate, which is a form of established knowledge about the state of the field.

claim: Dream frequency was reduced in patients with focal bilateral hippocampal damage compared to control participants.
source: Despite being roused a similar number of times, dream frequency was reduced in the patients compared to control participants, and the few dreams they reported were less episodic-like in nature and lacked content.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from the provoked awakening protocol and is shown in Figure 1D with statistical significance (p=0.028).

claim: Patients with focal bilateral hippocampal damage were roused a similar number of times as control participants.
source: Despite being roused a similar number of times, dream frequency was reduced in the patients compared to control participants, and the few dreams they reported were less episodic-like in nature and lacked content.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1B and Table 2, showing no significant difference in number of awakenings.

claim: The few dreams reported by patients with hippocampal damage were less episodic-like in nature compared to control participants.
source: Despite being roused a similar number of times, dream frequency was reduced in the patients compared to control participants, and the few dreams they reported were less episodic-like in nature and lacked content.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing patients had significantly fewer internal (episodic) details (p=0.028) as shown in Table 2.

claim: The few dreams reported by patients with hippocampal damage lacked content compared to control participants.
source: Despite being roused a similar number of times, dream frequency was reduced in the patients compared to control participants, and the few dreams they reported were less episodic-like in nature and lacked content.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing significantly lower content scores in patients (p=0.018) as shown in Figure 1E and Table 2.

claim: Hippocampal integrity may be necessary for typical dreaming to occur.
source: These results suggest that hippocampal integrity may be necessary for typical dreaming to occur, and aligns dreaming with other hippocampal-dependent processes such as episodic memory that are central to supporting our mental life.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental data showing reduced and degraded dreaming in hippocampal-damaged patients.

claim: Dreaming aligns with other hippocampal-dependent processes such as episodic memory.
source: These results suggest that hippocampal integrity may be necessary for typical dreaming to occur, and aligns dreaming with other hippocampal-dependent processes such as episodic memory that are central to supporting our mental life.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental findings and established knowledge about hippocampal function in episodic memory.

claim: Dreaming is defined as an internally-generated subjective mental experience during the sleep state.
source: Defined as an internally-generated subjective mental experience during the sleep state (Cipolli et al., 2017), dreaming can be present at initial sleep onset (hypnagogic sleep; Horikawa et al., 2013; Stickgold et al., 2000), during non-rapid eye movement (NREM) sleep (Antrobus et al., 1995; Foulkes, 1962; Nielsen, 2000; Siclari et al., 2017; Wamsley, 2013; Wamsley et al., 2007), and rapid eye movement (REM) sleep (Hobson et al., 2000; Maquet et al., 2000; Maquet et al., 2005).
evidence: This definition is supported by citation to Cipolli et al., 2017.

claim: Dreaming can be present at initial sleep onset (hypnagogic sleep).
source: Defined as an internally-generated subjective mental experience during the sleep state (Cipolli et al., 2017), dreaming can be present at initial sleep onset (hypnagogic sleep; Horikawa et al., 2013; Stickgold et al., 2000), during non-rapid eye movement (NREM) sleep (Antrobus et al., 1995; Foulkes, 1962; Nielsen, 2000; Siclari et al., 2017; Wamsley, 2013; Wamsley et al., 2007), and rapid eye movement (REM) sleep (Hobson et al., 2000; Maquet et al., 2000; Maquet et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Horikawa et al., 2013 and Stickgold et al., 2000.

claim: Dreaming can occur during non-rapid eye movement (NREM) sleep.
source: Defined as an internally-generated subjective mental experience during the sleep state (Cipolli et al., 2017), dreaming can be present at initial sleep onset (hypnagogic sleep; Horikawa et al., 2013; Stickgold et al., 2000), during non-rapid eye movement (NREM) sleep (Antrobus et al., 1995; Foulkes, 1962; Nielsen, 2000; Siclari et al., 2017; Wamsley, 2013; Wamsley et al., 2007), and rapid eye movement (REM) sleep (Hobson et al., 2000; Maquet et al., 2000; Maquet et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations: Antrobus et al., 1995; Foulkes, 1962; Nielsen, 2000; Siclari et al., 2017; Wamsley, 2013; Wamsley et al., 2007.

claim: Dreaming can occur during rapid eye movement (REM) sleep.
source: Defined as an internally-generated subjective mental experience during the sleep state (Cipolli et al., 2017), dreaming can be present at initial sleep onset (hypnagogic sleep; Horikawa et al., 2013; Stickgold et al., 2000), during non-rapid eye movement (NREM) sleep (Antrobus et al., 1995; Foulkes, 1962; Nielsen, 2000; Siclari et al., 2017; Wamsley, 2013; Wamsley et al., 2007), and rapid eye movement (REM) sleep (Hobson et al., 2000; Maquet et al., 2000; Maquet et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Hobson et al., 2000; Maquet et al., 2000; Maquet et al., 2005.

claim: Dreams are not a precise replay of our memories.
source: Although dreams are not a precise replay of our memories (Fosse et al., 2003; Stickgold et al., 2001a), it has been proposed that dreaming may be associated with memory consolidation processes (Payne, 2010; Wamsley, 2014; Wamsley et al., 2010; Wamsley and Stickgold, 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Fosse et al., 2003 and Stickgold et al., 2001a.

claim: It has been proposed that dreaming may be associated with memory consolidation processes.
source: Although dreams are not a precise replay of our memories (Fosse et al., 2003; Stickgold et al., 2001a), it has been proposed that dreaming may be associated with memory consolidation processes (Payne, 2010; Wamsley, 2014; Wamsley et al., 2010; Wamsley and Stickgold, 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Payne, 2010; Wamsley, 2014; Wamsley et al., 2010; Wamsley and Stickgold, 2019.

claim: In rodents and humans, patterns of brain activity exhibited during a learning experience were found to be subsequently expressed during sleep.
source: Indeed, in rodents and humans, patterns of brain activity exhibited during a learning experience were found to be subsequently expressed during sleep (Peigneux et al., 2004; Wilson and McNaughton, 1994).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Peigneux et al., 2004 and Wilson and McNaughton, 1994.

claim: Bilateral damage to the hippocampus adversely affects memory processing.
source: Bilateral damage to a brain structure called the hippocampus is known to adversely affect memory processing (Miller et al., 2017; Miller et al., 2020; Scoville and Milner, 1957; Spiers et al., 2001) and daydreaming (McCormick et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Miller et al., 2017; Miller et al., 2020; Scoville and Milner, 1957; Spiers et al., 2001.

claim: Bilateral damage to the hippocampus adversely affects daydreaming.
source: Bilateral damage to a brain structure called the hippocampus is known to adversely affect memory processing (Miller et al., 2017; Miller et al., 2020; Scoville and Milner, 1957; Spiers et al., 2001) and daydreaming (McCormick et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citation to McCormick et al., 2018.

claim: Some studies have reported repetitious and stereotyped dreams in patients with hippocampal lesions.
source: While sleep dreaming has been examined previously in patients with hippocampal lesions, results are mixed, with some studies reporting repetitious and stereotyped dreams (Torda, 1969a; Torda, 1969b; Stickgold et al., 2000), whereas others claim that hippocampal damage has no effect on dreaming (Solms, 1997; Solms, 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Torda, 1969a; Torda, 1969b; Stickgold et al., 2000.

claim: Some studies claim that hippocampal damage has no effect on dreaming.
source: While sleep dreaming has been examined previously in patients with hippocampal lesions, results are mixed, with some studies reporting repetitious and stereotyped dreams (Torda, 1969a; Torda, 1969b; Stickgold et al., 2000), whereas others claim that hippocampal damage has no effect on dreaming (Solms, 1997; Solms, 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Solms, 1997 and Solms, 2013.

claim: Previous studies on dreaming in hippocampal lesion patients have produced mixed results.
source: While sleep dreaming has been examined previously in patients with hippocampal lesions, results are mixed, with some studies reporting repetitious and stereotyped dreams (Torda, 1969a; Torda, 1969b; Stickgold et al., 2000), whereas others claim that hippocampal damage has no effect on dreaming (Solms, 1997; Solms, 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations showing contradictory findings from different studies.

claim: Differences in sleep stages sampled may explain disparate findings in previous studies of dreaming in hippocampal lesion patients.
source: Possible reasons for these disparate findings include differences in the sleep stages sampled, the inclusion in several studies of patients with psychiatric conditions and below-average IQ and, in other instances, patients were interviewed at a point temporally remote from any dreaming that might have occurred, presenting a challenge for these patients who usually suffer from amnesia.
evidence: This is an inference about methodological issues in previous studies.

claim: The inclusion of patients with psychiatric conditions and below-average IQ may explain disparate findings in previous studies of dreaming in hippocampal lesion patients.
source: Possible reasons for these disparate findings include differences in the sleep stages sampled, the inclusion in several studies of patients with psychiatric conditions and below-average IQ and, in other instances, patients were interviewed at a point temporally remote from any dreaming that might have occurred, presenting a challenge for these patients who usually suffer from amnesia.
evidence: This is an inference about methodological issues in previous studies.

claim: Interviewing patients at a point temporally remote from dreaming presents a challenge for patients who suffer from amnesia.
source: Possible reasons for these disparate findings include differences in the sleep stages sampled, the inclusion in several studies of patients with psychiatric conditions and below-average IQ and, in other instances, patients were interviewed at a point temporally remote from any dreaming that might have occurred, presenting a challenge for these patients who usually suffer from amnesia.
evidence: This is an inference based on knowledge about amnesia and memory retention.

claim: It remains uncertain whether hippocampal integrity is necessary for dreaming to occur.
source: It remains uncertain, therefore, whether hippocampal integrity is necessary for dreaming to occur.
evidence: This acknowledges the state of knowledge in the field based on the mixed previous findings.

claim: If bilateral hippocampal damage degrades dreaming, this would reinforce the link between dreaming and hippocampal-dependent processes such as memory.
source: If, as we predicted, bilateral hippocampal damage degrades dreaming, this would reinforce the link between dreaming and hippocampal-dependent processes such as memory, potentially moving us closer to an understanding of why we dream.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about the implications of the predicted findings.

claim: If hippocampal-damaged patients can have complex, imagery-rich, spatio-temporal mental events during sleep despite reduced ability during wake, this would need to be explicitly accounted for within theories of hippocampal function.
source: By contrast, if hippocampal-damaged patients who have a reduced ability to experience complex, imagery-rich, spatio-temporal mental events during wake are nevertheless able to have such experiences during sleep, this would need to be explicitly accounted for within theories of hippocampal function.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about alternative implications if the findings were different.

claim: Hippocampal-damaged patients have a reduced ability to experience complex, imagery-rich, spatio-temporal mental events during wake.
source: By contrast, if hippocampal-damaged patients who have a reduced ability to experience complex, imagery-rich, spatio-temporal mental events during wake are nevertheless able to have such experiences during sleep, this would need to be explicitly accounted for within theories of hippocampal function.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about hippocampal function.

claim: The study employed a provoked awakening protocol to examine sleep mentation.
source: Here, we sought to mitigate the issues affecting previous studies while investigating the frequency, features and content of dreaming in rare patients with selective bilateral hippocampal damage and matched control participants. To do this we employed a provoked awakening protocol (Nguyen et al., 2013; Siclari et al., 2013; Wamsley et al., 2016).
evidence: This describes the methodology used in the study, supported by citations to previous uses of this protocol.

claim: The provoked awakening protocol is a widely-used approach.
source: This widely-used approach involved waking participants up at various times during their night's sleep to report their thoughts in that moment.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about the methodology.

claim: The provoked awakening protocol involves waking participants up at various times during their night's sleep to report their thoughts in that moment.
source: This widely-used approach involved waking participants up at various times during their night's sleep to report their thoughts in that moment.
evidence: This describes the methodology used in the study.

claim: Four patients with selective bilateral hippocampal lesions and a specific episodic memory deficit were assessed.
source: We assessed four patients (all right-handed males; mean age 58.25 years, SD ±20.82) with selective bilateral hippocampal lesions and a specific episodic memory deficit (Table 1, Material and methods, Supplementary file 1, Spanò et al., 2020).
evidence: This describes the patient sample in the study.

claim: All four patients were right-handed males with a mean age of 58.25 years (SD ±20.82).
source: We assessed four patients (all right-handed males; mean age 58.25 years, SD ±20.82) with selective bilateral hippocampal lesions and a specific episodic memory deficit (Table 1, Material and methods, Supplementary file 1, Spanò et al., 2020).
evidence: This describes demographic characteristics of the patient sample.

claim: Patients were matched to ten healthy control participants who were all right-handed males with a mean age of 59.2 years (SD ±15.89).
source: Patients were matched to ten healthy control participants (all right-handed males; mean age 59.2 years, SD ±15.89) based on a number of demographic factors including age, gender, body mass index, non-verbal IQ, and a range of sleep quality measures (Table 1; Material and methods, Supplementary file 1, Supplementary file 2).
evidence: This describes the control sample in the study.

claim: Patients were matched to control participants based on age, gender, body mass index, non-verbal IQ, and a range of sleep quality measures.
source: Patients were matched to ten healthy control participants (all right-handed males; mean age 59.2 years, SD ±15.89) based on a number of demographic factors including age, gender, body mass index, non-verbal IQ, and a range of sleep quality measures (Table 1; Material and methods, Supplementary file 1, Supplementary file 2).
evidence: This describes the matching procedure used in the study design.

claim: In-home sleep recording was conducted using portable polysomnography on two consecutive nights.
source: We conducted in-home sleep recording using portable polysomnography (PSG) on two consecutive nights – one habituation night to allow for familiarization with the PSG equipment and one experimental night for the collection of dream reports.
evidence: This describes the methodology used in the study.

claim: One night was a habituation night to allow for familiarization with the PSG equipment.
source: We conducted in-home sleep recording using portable polysomnography (PSG) on two consecutive nights – one habituation night to allow for familiarization with the PSG equipment and one experimental night for the collection of dream reports.
evidence: This describes the study protocol.

claim: One night was an experimental night for the collection of dream reports.
source: We conducted in-home sleep recording using portable polysomnography (PSG) on two consecutive nights – one habituation night to allow for familiarization with the PSG equipment and one experimental night for the collection of dream reports.
evidence: This describes the study protocol.

claim: During the dream sampling night, participants were woken up after a period of 3 min from the onset of either NREM or REM sleep at various times throughout the night.
source: During the dream sampling night, participants were woken up after a period of 3 min from the onset of either NREM or REM sleep at various times throughout the night (Materials and methods, Figure 1A).
evidence: This describes the methodology used in the study, illustrated in Figure 1A.

claim: The number of total awakenings was not different between the patients and control participants.
source: The number of awakenings was not different between patients and control participants (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1B and Table 2 (p=0.829).

claim: There were no significant group differences in the proportion of awakenings from NREM and REM sleep.
source: Furthermore, there were no significant group differences in the proportion of awakenings from NREM and REM sleep (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1C and Table 2 (NREM: p=0.383; REM: p=0.309).

claim: The amount of probing did not differ between groups.
source: The amount of probing did not differ between groups.
evidence: This is supported by data in Table 2 showing no significant difference in number of probes per awakening (p=0.671).

claim: One patient did not report any dreams at all.
source: Of note, one patient did not report any dreams at all, but instead typically stated 'I can't picture it' (Figure 2).
evidence: This is supported by individual patient data shown in Figure 2 and Table 2.

claim: There was a significant difference between patients and controls for no dreams.
source: Although there was a significant difference between patients and controls for dreams (see above) and for no dreams, they did not differ in terms of the proportion of blank dreams, which was low for both groups.
evidence: This is supported by data in Table 2 showing a significant difference in proportion of no dreams (p=0.022).

claim: Patients and controls did not differ in terms of the proportion of blank dreams.
source: Although there was a significant difference between patients and controls for dreams (see above) and for no dreams, they did not differ in terms of the proportion of blank dreams, which was low for both groups.
evidence: This is supported by data in Table 2 showing no significant difference in proportion of blank dreams (p=0.496).

claim: The proportion of blank dreams was low for both groups.
source: Although there was a significant difference between patients and controls for dreams (see above) and for no dreams, they did not differ in terms of the proportion of blank dreams, which was low for both groups.
evidence: This is supported by data in Table 2 showing low proportions of blank dreams (HPC: 0.13; CTL: 0.12).

claim: Patients could distinguish between situations when they did not dream and those when they dreamt but could not remember.
source: This suggests that patients could distinguish between situations when they did not dream and those when they dreamt but could not remember.
evidence: This is an inference based on the finding that patients had different proportions of 'no dreams' versus 'blank dreams'.

claim: No validated objective measure of dreaming exists.
source: However, no validated objective measure of dreaming exists, and this should be borne in mind when interpreting participants' subjective reports.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about the limitations of dream research.

claim: These particular patients could retain information over several minutes in previous studies.
source: It is notable that in previous studies, these particular patients could retain information over several minutes, including reporting on their daydreaming (e.g. McCormick et al., 2016; McCormick et al., 2018), which speaks against a rapid decay of sleep mentation as an explanation for their reduced dream frequency.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies of these same patients.

claim: The ability of patients to retain information over several minutes speaks against rapid decay of sleep mentation as an explanation for their reduced dream frequency.
source: It is notable that in previous studies, these particular patients could retain information over several minutes, including reporting on their daydreaming (e.g. McCormick et al., 2016; McCormick et al., 2018), which speaks against a rapid decay of sleep mentation as an explanation for their reduced dream frequency.
evidence: This is an inference based on previous findings about these patients' memory abilities.

claim: One patient had no dreams whatsoever and was not included in analyses of dream features and content.
source: Because one patient had no dreams whatsoever, he was not included in these analyses.
evidence: This describes the analytical approach used in the study.

claim: While the patients used fewer informative words, overall there was no significant difference between the groups.
source: We first examined the number of informative words (see Materials and methods; Stickgold et al., 2001b) used in the dream narratives and, while the patients used fewer such words, overall there was no significant difference between the groups.
evidence: This is supported by data in Table 2 showing no significant difference in number of informative words (p=0.176).

claim: Bilateral hippocampal damage does not affect narrative construction or verbal descriptive ability.
source: A number of studies addressed this concern during tasks involving the imagination of scenes or future scenarios, counterfactual thinking, describing the present and pictures of scenes. Bilateral hippocampal damage does not affect narrative construction or verbal descriptive ability (e.g. Race et al., 2011; Race et al., 2013; Mullally et al., 2012; Mullally and Maguire, 2014; Miller et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to multiple studies.

claim: The patients in the current study had no difficulty performing verbal fluency tests or other tasks where total word count was measured.
source: Considering specifically the patients in the current study, they too had no difficulty performing verbal fluency tests or other tasks where total word count was measured (Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is supported by data in Supplementary file 1.

claim: It is unlikely that the patients' performance was driven by an underlying expressive verbal problem.
source: Given these general and specific findings, it is unlikely that the patients' performance was driven by an underlying expressive verbal problem.
evidence: This is an inference based on the verbal ability data from this and previous studies.

claim: There were no significant group differences in terms of general complexity of dream reports.
source: Next we assessed overall qualitative features of dream reports using experimenter ratings (Materials and methods; De Gennaro et al., 2011; Oudiette et al., 2012). There were no significant group differences in terms of general complexity, vividness, bizarreness, emotional valence (there were no nightmares), and proportion of self-references.
evidence: This is supported by data in Table 2 showing no significant difference in complexity (p=0.098).

claim: There were no significant group differences in terms of vividness of dream reports.
source: Next we assessed overall qualitative features of dream reports using experimenter ratings (Materials and methods; De Gennaro et al., 2011; Oudiette et al., 2012). There were no significant group differences in terms of general complexity, vividness, bizarreness, emotional valence (there were no nightmares), and proportion of self-references.
evidence: This is supported by data in Table 2 showing no significant difference in vividness (p=0.203).

claim: There were no significant group differences in terms of bizarreness of dream reports.
source: Next we assessed overall qualitative features of dream reports using experimenter ratings (Materials and methods; De Gennaro et al., 2011; Oudiette et al., 2012). There were no significant group differences in terms of general complexity, vividness, bizarreness, emotional valence (there were no nightmares), and proportion of self-references.
evidence: This is supported by data in Table 2 showing no significant difference in bizarreness (p=0.232).

claim: There were no significant group differences in terms of emotional valence of dream reports.
source: Next we assessed overall qualitative features of dream reports using experimenter ratings (Materials and methods; De Gennaro et al., 2011; Oudiette et al., 2012). There were no significant group differences in terms of general complexity, vividness, bizarreness, emotional valence (there were no nightmares), and proportion of self-references.
evidence: This is supported by data in Table 2 showing no significant difference in emotional valence (p=0.720).

claim: There were no nightmares reported.
source: Next we assessed overall qualitative features of dream reports using experimenter ratings (Materials and methods; De Gennaro et al., 2011; Oudiette et al., 2012). There were no significant group differences in terms of general complexity, vividness, bizarreness, emotional valence (there were no nightmares), and proportion of self-references.
evidence: This is a direct observation from the data.

claim: There were no significant group differences in terms of proportion of self-references in dream reports.
source: Next we assessed overall qualitative features of dream reports using experimenter ratings (Materials and methods; De Gennaro et al., 2011; Oudiette et al., 2012). There were no significant group differences in terms of general complexity, vividness, bizarreness, emotional valence (there were no nightmares), and proportion of self-references.
evidence: This is supported by data in Table 2 showing no significant difference in proportion of self-references (p=1.000).

claim: The patients included significantly fewer internal details in their dream narratives relative to controls.
source: The patients included significantly fewer internal details in their dream narratives relative to controls, whereas there was no significant group difference in terms of external details.
evidence: This is supported by data in Table 2 showing a significant difference in internal (episodic) details (p=0.028).

claim: There was no significant group difference in terms of external details in dream narratives.
source: The patients included significantly fewer internal details in their dream narratives relative to controls, whereas there was no significant group difference in terms of external details.
evidence: This is supported by data in Table 2 showing no significant difference in external (semantic/other) details (p=0.258).

claim: The dream reports of patients were significantly less rich in content compared to those of the control participants.
source: A second method, usually employed for scoring the content of imagined scenes (Hassabis et al., 2007), showed that the dream reports of patients were significantly less rich in content compared to those of the control participants (Figure 1E).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1E and Table 2 (p=0.018).

claim: The findings accord with previous studies that reported stereotyped dreaming in patients with brain damage that extended beyond the hippocampi.
source: By studying rare patients with selective bilateral hippocampal damage we found that dream frequency was reduced compared to control participants, and the few dreams they had were less episodic-like in nature and lacked content. This accords with previous studies that reported stereotyped dreaming in patients with brain damage that extended beyond the hippocampi (Torda, 1969a; Torda, 1969b; Stickgold et al., 2000), and echoes the effects of hippocampal damage on imagination (Hassabis et al., 2007), episodic memory (Miller et al., 2017; Miller et al., 2020; Spiers et al., 2001) and daydreaming (McCormick et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The findings echo the effects of hippocampal damage on imagination.
source: By studying rare patients with selective bilateral hippocampal damage we found that dream frequency was reduced compared to control participants, and the few dreams they had were less episodic-like in nature and lacked content. This accords with previous studies that reported stereotyped dreaming in patients with brain damage that extended beyond the hippocampi (Torda, 1969a; Torda, 1969b; Stickgold et al., 2000), and echoes the effects of hippocampal damage on imagination (Hassabis et al., 2007), episodic memory (Miller et al., 2017; Miller et al., 2020; Spiers et al., 2001) and daydreaming (McCormick et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Hassabis et al., 2007 and the current study's data.

claim: The findings echo the effects of hippocampal damage on episodic memory.
source: By studying rare patients with selective bilateral hippocampal damage we found that dream frequency was reduced compared to control participants, and the few dreams they had were less episodic-like in nature and lacked content. This accords with previous studies that reported stereotyped dreaming in patients with brain damage that extended beyond the hippocampi (Torda, 1969a; Torda, 1969b; Stickgold et al., 2000), and echoes the effects of hippocampal damage on imagination (Hassabis et al., 2007), episodic memory (Miller et al., 2017; Miller et al., 2020; Spiers et al., 2001) and daydreaming (McCormick et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Miller et al., 2017; Miller et al., 2020; Spiers et al., 2001 and the current study's data.

claim: The findings echo the effects of hippocampal damage on daydreaming.
source: By studying rare patients with selective bilateral hippocampal damage we found that dream frequency was reduced compared to control participants, and the few dreams they had were less episodic-like in nature and lacked content. This accords with previous studies that reported stereotyped dreaming in patients with brain damage that extended beyond the hippocampi (Torda, 1969a; Torda, 1969b; Stickgold et al., 2000), and echoes the effects of hippocampal damage on imagination (Hassabis et al., 2007), episodic memory (Miller et al., 2017; Miller et al., 2020; Spiers et al., 2001) and daydreaming (McCormick et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citation to McCormick et al., 2018 and the current study's data.

claim: Studies have shown that there is often continuity between waking life experiences and dreaming.
source: Despite the tendency to confine dreaming to the sleep state, studies have shown that there is often continuity between waking life experiences and dreaming (Andrillon et al., 2015; Fosse et al., 2003; Horikawa et al., 2013; Schredl and Hofmann, 2003).
evidence: This is supported by citations to multiple studies.

claim: The capacity to dream might have been intact but underused in the patients due to difficulty retaining information during wake.
source: Given that the patients had difficulty retaining information over longer time scales while awake, then perhaps during subsequent sleep there was little material to process. Hence it could be that the capacity to dream was intact, but underused, in the patients.
evidence: This is a speculative explanation for the findings.

claim: The core capacity for dreaming might have been compromised in the patients, which in turn affected memory processing.
source: Alternatively, the core capacity for dreaming might have been compromised, with this in turn affecting memory processing.
evidence: This is a speculative alternative explanation for the findings.

claim: Dreaming has been linked with the consolidation of information into long-term memory.
source: Dreaming has been linked with the consolidation of information into long-term memory (Payne, 2010; Wamsley, 2013; Wamsley, 2014; Wamsley et al., 2010; Wamsley and Stickgold, 2019), but it is unknown whether dreaming plays a functional role in this process (Wamsley, 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to multiple studies.

claim: It is unknown whether dreaming plays a functional role in memory consolidation.
source: Dreaming has been linked with the consolidation of information into long-term memory (Payne, 2010; Wamsley, 2013; Wamsley, 2014; Wamsley et al., 2010; Wamsley and Stickgold, 2019), but it is unknown whether dreaming plays a functional role in this process (Wamsley, 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Wamsley, 2014.

claim: If dreaming plays a functional role in memory consolidation, patients with hippocampal damage may lack this dream-related mechanism for facilitating memory processing, which could contribute to their amnesia.
source: If it does, then patients with hippocampal damage may lack this dream-related mechanism for facilitating memory processing, and this could contribute to their amnesia.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about potential mechanisms.

claim: Slow-wave sleep (SWS) is a stage within NREM sleep that has been associated with episodic memory consolidation.
source: Another aspect of sleep that has been associated with episodic memory consolidation is slow-wave sleep (SWS), a stage within NREM sleep (Rasch and Born, 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Rasch and Born, 2013.

claim: The hippocampal-damaged patients tested here had significantly reduced SWS and slow wave activity.
source: We have previously shown that the hippocampal-damaged patients tested here had significantly reduced SWS and slow wave activity, whereas the time spent in other sleep stages was comparable to that of control participants (Spanò et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a previous study of these same patients.

claim: The time spent in other sleep stages was comparable between patients and control participants.
source: We have previously shown that the hippocampal-damaged patients tested here had significantly reduced SWS and slow wave activity, whereas the time spent in other sleep stages was comparable to that of control participants (Spanò et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a previous study of these same patients.

claim: It is unlikely that the patients' degraded dreaming was caused solely by decreased SWS.
source: It is unlikely that the patients' degraded dreaming was caused solely by decreased SWS. This is because we sampled dreaming across both NREM and REM sleep, and of the dreams sampled during NREM sleep in the control participants, just 5% (SD 11.3) were during SWS.
evidence: This is an inference based on the study design and data showing that only 5% of NREM dreams in controls were during SWS.

claim: Of the dreams sampled during NREM sleep in the control participants, just 5% (SD 11.3) were during SWS.
